body_markdown:
Tires come in all shapes and sizes these days. Well, perhaps not shapes, but the compounds used to make these circular feats of engineering come in a diverse array of formulations. We have tires that are good in winter, some excel in the summer, and others are perfectly acceptable in any situation. This is a lot to juggle in a motorist’s mind, and I openly wondered what my co-workers here at Hagerty Media thought about this matter.


I was surprised to see my question was met with immediate responses. Apparently we all enjoy our daily drivers more than I anticipated! So have a look at what tires we run on our daily drivers, as we all have relevant thoughts on all-seasons and dedicated Summer or Winter tires.


## Pro Snow


Pixabay


“Ever since spending four winters in Traverse City, MI, I have relied on snow tires. I had a new Dodge Dart when I lived in the snowglobe up there, and it never failed me in those months. They made an underpowered, FWD car very livable in winter. Now I swear by them.


I swap Blizzaks onto my Focus ST every snowy season (often later than I should). They actually make driving that car in the winter nearly as fun as on the summertime Pilot Sports. I also mount the snow tires on the OEM rims and have aftermarket black OZ Racing rims for summer. Makes the swaps super easy. And, while running two sets of tires every year is expensive, it does extend the life of each set, so it evens out costwise.” — *Todd Kraemer*


“It has been a while since I lived in the frozen north of Michigan, but while I was there, my wife and I relied on our 4WD Chevy short-bed pickup, which was invariably ready for anything, and the general goodness of front-wheel drive on our Dodge Neon R/T.


But then I stumbled across a set of Bridgestone Blizzaks, mounted them on some steelies and put them on the Neon, and my life was forever changed—or if not my life, certainly my opinion of dedicated snow tires. They were just excellent, and completely negated the need for driving all four wheels. I had no idea how much better they would work than typical all-seasons, and if I ever move back, they’d be among my early purchases.” — *Steven Cole Smith*


“Northern Michigander here. I loathe that people think they can get away with ‘all-season’ tires up here. Granted, there are a few new all-weather tires that I hear relatively good things about, but when there’s snow and ice on the roads for nearly half the year, you owe it to yourself to have a proper set of snow tires. FWD plus snow tires will get you nearly anywhere you need to go up here. AWD/4WD with snow tires, and you can nearly drive like it’s dry pavement.


With all the highway miles I do with my family during the spring/summer/fall, it makes sense to have a good set of grand touring tires. In my case this also involves getting the XL version to handle the weight of 6 people, a full trunk, bike rack with 6-7 bikes, and two roof boxes packed full of gear!


Ben Woodworth


Lastly, I’m a huge fan of having a set of wheels for each set of tires. It allows me to easily swap things in my driveway when needed and not be in the seasonal tire shop panic after the first snow where it’s a 2-week wait to get your snows put on!” — *Ben Woodworth*


“Snow tire evangelist here. I’ve had so many one-wheel-drive cars do just fine in Ohio winters with the right set of rubber. I do enjoy a good rear-biased AWD vehicle in the winter, but it’s by no means necessary. My winter tech order of preference: 1) snow tires 2) limited-slip (FWD or RWD, doesn’t matter) 3) all-wheel drive.


And I second Ben’s note about having a wheel/tire set ready and just tossing them on when the time comes. It’s easy enough to find a used set of wheels out there. Addendum #2: Winter tires often ride better than summers. I enjoy the extra bit of cushion for the 5 months I’ve got my snows on.” — *Eddy Eckart*


“Longtime winter tire advocate here, also, which traces back to my career at Automobile Magazine, where we routinely had a ‘Four Seasons’ fleet of long-term (one year) test cars, all of which were religiously fitted with the latest and greatest winter rubber from November to April.


We have always applied the same thinking to our personal cars. That said, in recent years, the winters have been so mild here in Southeast Michigan that I sometimes find myself wishing and hoping for a good snowstorm, such that I can actually put my Michelin X Ice winter rubber to proper use. I know that the conditions are a totally different ballgame in northwest Michigan where my colleagues at Hagerty HQ are based.” — *Joe DeMatio*


## All The Way With All-Seasons


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


“My only all-season vehicle is my ’22 GMC Canyon AT4. The factory-installed Goodyear DuraTracs do the trick just fine in the deep Northern Michigan lake-effect snow as well as mall crawling in the summer. They do the trick, and truck tires are way expensive, so no, I just live with it.” **—** *Greg Ingold*


“All-seasons for me and my primary (Ford Ranger) here in Houston, TX. It would be tempting to put summer tires on it, because it’s so small/light/tossable, but I do need one vehicle with all-seasons on those infrequent days when we get sleet and possibly frozen overpasses. Then again, all my machinations are irrelevant, because I love my 15″ Alcoa wheels and nobody makes summer tires in my truck’s size!”— *Sajeev Mehta*


“Studded snow tires are legal where I am in the PNW, but they’re also mostly unnecessary for the majority of drivers (those who aren’t heading up to the mountain to ski every weekend), so of course the roads around town are full of people driving on them November–April. As result the asphalt and concrete surfaces get deep grooves worn into them. It’s so stupid. I have three-peak-rated A/T tires on one of my vehicles, and I carry chains in the winter, and that combination has never failed me.” — *Stefan Lombard*


## Summer Tires + Bonus Thoughts


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


“Back when my Lincoln Mark VIII was my daily driver—which was a long time ago—I learned to love the summer tire. It all started when I first used Tire Rack back in 1999, upgrading from a set of all-seasons to high-performance all-seasons. Wow, what a difference! Then I upgraded those to summer tires and was blown away at how fantastic they performed (in warm climates).


Summer tires make just about any vehicle better in temperatures above freezing. I love how grippy they are in turns, paired with the fantastic confidence and quiet ride you’d expect in an all-season tire. Sure, they don’t last as long, and they are likely terrifying in below-freezing temperatures, but that’s not a concern where I live. Even when it’s freezing outside, the ground is generally above freezing, but your experiences will vary.” — *Sajeev Mehta*


“I’m fortunate/unfortunate enough to live in a subtropical climate. ‘Winter’ in Southeast Texas involves snow or ice only once every few years, and it’s always brief, so for the truly cold days I just stock up ahead of time and then stay home. In other words, summer tires have always been perfectly fine down here, because summer basically lasts like nine months.” — *Andrew Newton*


“I will clarify that if I drove a car in the winter, I’d be on snows all day long. The last time I had a car as a daily, it was a 1982 Olds 98, and yeah that thing was a beast in the snow with the right tires, even with RWD and an open diff.” — *Greg Ingold*


“In my experience, cheap car + quality/expensive tires is better than good/expensive car paired with cheap, wrong, or worn tires.” — *Ben Woodworth*


“Oddly, they don’t make winter tires in[36 x 4 1/2](https://cokertire.com/universal-blackwall-36x4-5.html) so I’m forced to put on ‘summer’ tires. Besides the fact that I live in California, when you only have rear brakes, it doesn’t really make much difference what tire you put on.” — *Aaron Robinson*
